title: Line Breeding Rabbits: A Practical Genetics Guide
summary: How line breeding works, what it can accomplish, where the risks come from, and what records a breeder should keep before making related pairings.

title: Rabbit Genetics: From Genes to Breeding Decisions
summary: A ground-up guide to genes, alleles, dominant and recessive inheritance, Punnett squares, coat-color loci, hidden carriers, epistasis, pedigrees, polygenic traits, and practical breeding decisions.

title: Understanding Rabbit Pedigrees: How to Read One and What Actually Matters
summary: A pedigree is useful only when it helps a breeder understand ancestry, verify records, and make better decisions. This guide explains what to look for beyond a page full of names.

title: How to Choose a Breeding Pair: More Than Just Matching Pedigrees
summary: Choosing a breeding pair should start with a defined goal and evidence from the animals, their families, and their records—not simply two pedigrees that look good together.

title: Rabbit Color Genetics for Beginners
summary: Rabbit coat color becomes easier when you learn a few basic genetics terms, then study one locus at a time instead of trying to memorize every color combination.

title: Preparing for a Rabbit Litter: A Week-by-Week Breeding Timeline
summary: Good litter preparation is mostly recordkeeping, observation, and having the nest and supplies ready before the doe kindles.

title: What to Record for Every Animal in a Breeding Program
summary: Good records turn individual animals into usable breeding information. The goal is not to collect every possible detail—it is to preserve the information that changes decisions.

title: Line Breeding vs. Inbreeding vs. Outcrossing
summary: These breeding terms are often used as if they describe completely different genetic systems. In reality, they describe different relationship strategies and different levels of shared ancestry.

title: How to Evaluate a Rabbit Before Adding It to Your Breeding Program
summary: A breeding prospect should be evaluated as a whole animal: identity, health, structure, temperament, family history, reproductive potential, and how well it fits the program's actual goal.

title: How to Build a Breeding Program Instead of Just Producing Litters
summary: A breeding program has a direction, measurable selection criteria, records, and a plan for what happens after offspring are born. A series of matings without those pieces is simply reproduction.

title: Newborn Rabbit Kits: What’s Normal and What Needs Attention
summary: Newborn kits are fragile, but not every quiet nest is an emergency. The goal is to recognize normal early development and identify signs that need prompt intervention.

title: When Should You Retire a Breeding Rabbit?
summary: There is no universal retirement age for every breeding rabbit. Retirement should be based on health, fertility, condition, reproductive history, and the needs of the breeding program.

title: Understanding COI: Coefficient of Inbreeding Explained Without the Math Headache
summary: COI estimates how much of an animal's genome may be homozygous because both copies trace back to the same ancestor. It is a relationship tool—not a score for whether an animal is good or bad.

title: Keeping Accurate Medical Records for Livestock and Rabbits
summary: Medical records should tell the story of what was observed, what was diagnosed, what was done, and what happened afterward. Good records protect animal care and improve breeding decisions.

title: How to Track Litter Performance and Identify Your Best Breeding Lines
summary: Tracking litter performance turns reproduction into comparable data. The most useful line is not always the one with the largest litter—it is the line that consistently meets the program's complete goal.

title: Genotype vs. Phenotype: Why an Animal Can Carry Traits You Can’t See
summary: Phenotype is what you observe. Genotype is the genetic information behind the animal. Understanding the difference explains hidden recessives, unexpected offspring, and why appearance alone cannot predict every mating.

title: Common Pedigree Mistakes—and How They Affect a Breeding Program
summary: Pedigree errors do more than make a document look sloppy. They can distort relationship calculations, genetic assumptions, ownership history, and future breeding decisions.

title: Breeding for Improvement: How to Identify Strengths and Faults Across Generations
summary: Real genetic improvement is a pattern across generations, not a single exceptional animal. This guide shows how to separate family strengths from one-off results.

title: What Makes a Good Breeding Record?
summary: A good breeding record preserves the full reproductive history: what was attempted, when it happened, what the result was, and what the breeder learned.

title: Selecting Replacement Stock: Which Young Animals Should You Keep?
summary: Replacement selection should be based on the breeding program's future needs, not simply which young animal catches your eye first.

title: Quarantine Protocols When Bringing a New Animal Into Your Herd or Rabbitry
summary: Quarantine reduces the chance that a new arrival introduces disease into an established group. It works only when separation includes animals, equipment, people, records, and a clear release decision.

title: Why Breeders Should Track Failed Breedings Too
summary: Failed breedings are not empty records. They can reveal fertility decline, management problems, seasonal effects, pair-specific issues, or health concerns that successful breeding records alone cannot show.
